STUDENTS AND FACULTY HAVE DESIGNED AND CONSTRUCTED THE MAIN STUDY BUILDING OF BLACK MOUNTAIN COLLEGE
INFORMAL CLASSES are usual at the college. Students wear casual work clothes, girls prefer to roll their blue jeans or else wear shorts. Classes are held in the Main Studies building or in faculty homes. Here, Prof. Strauss conducts discussion in philosophy.
INDIVIDUAL STUDY ROOMS are allotted each student in the Main Building. The rooms are furnished by the students, used to work after classes. The faculty have similar studies to use for their own projects. The students do not sleep here but live in dorms.
The College That Built Itself
Black Mountain points its program to the future
Ten years ago, a group of rebellious educators pooled their resources and went back into the mountains of western North Carolina to found a new kind of college. They were men who opposed the study courses and graduation credit system existing in most American universities. They were dissatisfied with standard methods of teaching. They felt that higher education had lost its basic purpose- to train students for leadership in the nation as well as a job in life.
The result was Black Mountain College, an experiment in education, a blueprint for democracy at work. It’s a college which has been built, in main, by its students and faculty and not by financial grants and endowments.
Despite chronic financial crises, Black Mountain continues to grow in reputation as well as in size, although it has not prospered. In the post-war world, this college may take the lead in pointing the way to a new type of training for our youth.
If the war is to mean anything, it must lead the way to a greater regard of man for his fellow-man. Paradoxically, that job begins on the battlefields of the world. But it must also be done in the schools and colleges. To educate is not enough. Youth must be trained in cooperation and democracy.
Black Mountain tries to do the job in two ways. It educates through an interrelated program of subjects where the influence of history on literature is covered in a single course, where philosophy and the social sciences become a study of man’s problems in the terms of the student’s own experiences. It trains through a work program which teaches students the proper use of tools, gives them a community sense and responsibility about their work.
When the faculty and students first came to Black Mountain, it had a few small buildings, formerly part of a summer hotel, which inadequately housed the college. Since then, both faculty and students participating in the work program have constructed twelve buildings, cultivated a farm, built tennis courts. They designed the plans, cut the lumber, formed the cement blocks for their modern main study building. In blue jeans and work clothes, piling into college trucks, the students and teachers together built a college where no college had been.
That the program of Black Mountain has been successful is evident in the way students speak about the college. Twenty-one-year-old Bob Marden, a senior, sums it up this way:
“You change when you come here. It may take a long time; it may take three or four days. But after a while you feel the community spirit here and soon you start saying, ‘we built this and we did that’!”
Persons who talk like that know what democracy means. They know it means freedom buy they also know it mean responsibility.
Black Mountain is not a rich man’s college nor does it pay high salaries to its faculty. Less than 50 per cent of the students pay the full fee of $1200 for room, board and tuition. In the past ten years, the college annually has allotted $30,000 of its limited budget for scholarships. You can’t “work your way through” Black Mountain. But if the faculty admissions committee believes in your ability, the tuition scale can slide down to nothing.
When the faculty of a college votes to take new salary cuts- as they did at Black Mountain- while increasing the scholarship fund, then you know you’ve found a school which can’t die, a school which will continue to build itself into a highly important institution.
STUDENTS BEGIN CLEARING LAND FOR A NEW PROJECT
CONCERTS, ART EXHIBITIONS, guest lectures are held frequently in the college dining hall which is converted into a grand salon for special occasions. Plays are presented here by the college group. Saturday nights students and faculty hold a semi-formal dance.

THE COLLEGE THAT BUILT ITSELF continued
W. ROBERT WUNSCH ELSA KAHL THEODORE DREIER HEINRICH JALOWETZ
KENNETH KURTZ A. LAWRENCE KOCHER JOSEF ALBERS FRITZ J. HANSGIRG
Outstanding Men and Women Staff the College
W. ROBERT WUNSCH, college rector, is administrative head elected by the faculty. One of the original founders, Wunsch teaches dramatics, is an authority on Negro educational problems in the South. KENNETH KURTZ gives English and American literature. A former Rhodes scholar, he previously taught at Cal. Tech. ELSA KAHL, leading director of the Ballet Jooss, came to teach “eukinetics”- a study of motion-when ballet disbanded last year. Her husband, Frederic Cohen, ballet music director, also teaches. A. LAWRENCE KOCHER, one of America’s top architects, has courses in design, supervises all college construction. THEODORE DREIER, also one of the original group which founded Black Mountain College in 1933, teaches mathematics, was formerly at Rollins College. JOSEF ALBERS, art professor, taught at the Bauhaus, Germany, until its closing by Hitler. He is assembling a color exhibit of college work for Museum of Modern Art. HEINRICH JALOWETZ, one of pre-Nazi Europe’s outstanding conductors, teaches music composition and form at the college. FRITZ J. HANSGIRG, professor of physical sciences, was paroled by FBI to college after war broke. Classified as enemy alien, he was designing magnesium plants for Henry Kaiser.
A HUNDRED-ACRE FARM, tilled by volunteer labor of students and professors, supplies the college with vegetables, milk, and some meat. It is an integral part of the practical work program which teaches students responsibility to the community and familiarity with everyday work tools. College work program varies from construction, pasture clearance, and road repair to electric wiring, cabinet making. Students put in three days each week on the work program. Since no student can pay for tuition by working, the program has a real educational value.
“WERKLEHRE” is what Professor Albers calls his classes in art design. Students have an unlimited choice of materials- textiles, leaves, paints- to develop an understanding of the subject. Like almost all other courses of study at Black Mountain College, art classes are flexible, do not confine themselves solely to one phase of art. Weaving looms in foreground of photo are used both for practical work and design study.
LABORATORY EQUIPMENT and scientific apparatus is used by students for elementary work in physics and undergraduate work in chemistry and biology. Equipment is housed in long, one-story wooden building built by the students. Science department is concentrating on war work.
POST-WAR PLANNING CLASSES are not confined to social studies but include practical work in architecture. Here, designer Kocher explains the model for a post-war pre-fabricated home which can be constructed for $1500 on a mass production scale. Classes at college are usually small.
